title: Case 29 of the Gateless Gate
speaker: Heather Shoren Larusso
summary: The talk's main teaching is about cultivating a detached awareness by stopping attachment to thoughts and perceptions. This means letting go of our fixed views and investigating what's truly perceiving them, rather than getting caught up in dualistic analysis or identifying with thinking. By doing so, we can tap into the wisdom that animates all things, including ourselves and others, and find a common ground beyond our individual perspectives.

Heather was ordained in 2015 at Brooklyn Zen Center.
She's also had 12 practice periods at Tassajara.

Thank you very much, Heather, for coming to us in our living rooms.
I'm looking forward to your talk.
Thank you very much.
Thank you, Chris.
Thank you, Chris, for inviting me to give the Dharma talk from the comfort of our living rooms or bedrooms or dining rooms, wherever we may be right now.
And I so appreciate everyone being here on a Sunday morning.
I hope you are all doing well and staying safe and connected during these times that are very trying, this past year of lots of division in our country and also in our world.
I'm going to speak about a case, an ancient case from the Gateless Gate.
It's case 29.
When I read these koans, I try to see how they apply to my 21st century life, and this one I find to be particularly instructive.
I remember when I first read this koan, it's probably 2005 or 2006.
I bought one of those little books, Zen in a nutshell books, and it had koans and some haiku.
For some reason, this particular koan, I remember it, maybe because I was so confused by it.
So I'd like to talk about this koan and my understanding of it, and at the end, we can have a conversation about it.
Whenever a teacher came to a temple, or there was going to be a Dharma talk by the resident teacher, at the monasteries they'd raise a flag, right?
So there were these two monks outside of the temple, and they were looking at the flag, flapping in the wind.
One monk said that the flag is moving.
The other monk says, "Oh, the wind is moving."
And there they are, they get into this heated argument about whether the wind is moving or whether the flag is moving.
And they couldn't reach a conclusion about which was correct.
The sixth ancestor, who is Huineng, walks by and overhears these two monks arguing about the wind and the flag.
He walks past and he says, "It's not the wind that moves, it's not the flag that moves, it is your mind that moves."
And the two monks were awestruck.
The classical understanding of this koan, again, case 29 from the Gateless Gate, is, to sum up in a couple of words, the grand master of Zen's teaching: stop clinging, drop views, investigate mind.
These monks are so caught up in defending their points of view that they fail to notice their basic misperceptions.
Huineng is chastising these monks and saying, if your mind wasn't so discursive, if your mind wasn't moving, you wouldn't get caught in arguing about these forms.
These forms are empty, these forms are transitory, the forms being the wind and the flag, and also the mind, even though it's not material.
Are these empty objects important enough to get all riled up about?
They were attached to their points of view, these two monks.

They had no idea they were identified with thinking mind and that they were relating to the flag and to the wind as if those objects of mind are substantial and independent of their own sensory apparatus.
They're identified with delusive thinking, and that is agitating their bodies and their minds.
They're also caught up in the linguistic concepts of flag and wind.
By reifying or concretizing these sensory objects, the monks are also reifying themselves.
They fail to take the backward step and investigate the one that's perceiving.
Both the mind that's perceiving and the object of perception are in constant flux.
The monks also fail to remember.
The word is sati, S-A-T-I, right, like sati, patana, sutta.
They're failing to recollect, right, the memory.
They're not remembering that the flag, wind, and mind are all suffused with buddha nature, that the essence of mind, emptiness, does not move, right, shunyata does not move.

So Huineng uses skillful means to slice through the monks' fixation on sensory experience, most especially trying to remind them with his Manjushri sword to take the backward step and investigate thinking mind.
He uses words to go beyond words.
It's just a little bit about Huineng.

He lived in China from 638 to 713 during the Tang dynasty, and he's considered the founder of the Southern School of Zen, which is what we would say is the sudden enlightenment school of Zen, as opposed to the Northern School, which was a gradual enlightenment.
The fifth ancestor, Hongren, discovered when Huineng came to his monastery that Huineng was an illiterate commoner from the south.
Huineng was in the north of China, and Hongren realized that this illiterate woodcutter wanted to pursue the buddha nature, to learn about the buddha mind.
So Hongren says to Huineng, "You are a barbarian.
How could you hope for becoming a buddha?"
And Huineng responds, "A barbarian is only apparently different from you, but there is no distinction concerning our buddha nature."
This also, of course, is what he's saying to these two monks who are arguing about flag and wind.
Their minds are making the distinctions, which obviously, mind needs to make distinctions, otherwise we might try to drive a tree and might try to water a car.
So clearly, dualistic thinking is helpful, and obviously, it also can get us into trouble because it continues to divide the world and divide ourselves.

Huineng actually receives the robe and the bowl and the transmission of the buddha mind from Hongren, and he flees Hongren's monastery because the other monks were jealous and did not feel that this illiterate woodcutter should actually be Hongren's Dharma heir.
The legend is that Huineng disappeared into the forest for 10 years and that he traveled around with a nomadic band of hunters.
I also read that it could have been thieves, so either bandits or hunters, I'm not sure, or maybe a combination of both.
And this is the first koan that he gave.
This is his first teaching after emerging from his stay in the forest.
When Huineng was a boy, he heard somebody chanting the Diamond Sutra while he was walking through a village, and this is the verse that he woke up to:
*Bodhisattva, mahasattvas should generate a pure mind thus.
They should not activate the mind dwelling on form.
They should not activate the mind dwelling on sound, scent, flavor, feeling, or phenomena.
They should activate the mind without dwelling on anything.*
Huineng says when the mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure.
This means always working with moments of thought, which is what those two monks weren't doing, right?
They were relating to form and wind as if form and wind were substantial and independent, not interdependent.
Their minds were being activated when they were dwelling on these forms, right?
They were attaching to points of view, right and wrong, flag versus wind.
This is a deluded person.
The deluded person is the one who substantiates these objects of perception.
And as you know, the mind's thoughts are also objects of perception, the mentality.
If you are detached from forms, however, even as you see forms, so if I'm detached from flag and wind even as I see them, then the mind is activated without dwelling on forms.
This is what they would say is an enlightened person.
The key phrase here is "without dwelling" or "unsupported."
In Sanskrit, this word is apratishita, which the Buddhist scholar Edward Ikanze translates in several ways.
As applied to relations between two objects, flag and wind, it's not relying on anything, not getting carried away by anything, and not clinging to anything, which clearly these monks were doing.
If you apply this word to emotional experience, it's not settling down anywhere, not grasping onto that mood, not making oneself at home anywhere, and not seeking a secure base anywhere.
If you apply it to a social relationship, Ikanze says it's not expecting any help from anything, not trusting in anything, except, of course, perfect wisdom, prajnaparamita.
It's not believing in anything blindly.
Huineng reminds these monks that they're stuck in delusion and suffering because they are dwelling on forms.
They are not working with Buddha mind in every moment of thought.
The main teaching of the Diamond Sutra is that the essence of mind, emptiness, or Buddha nature does not fluctuate.
In the Mahayana prajnaparamita sutras, Buddha mind is equal to emptiness.
The small mind flaps like the flag, buffeted by the breeze of karmic conditioning.
We get so caught up in our perceptions as being right that we miss the totality of interdependence, the constancy of change, and the impersonal nature of suffering.
And yes, of course, there's a flag, and there's wind, and there's monks, and there's small minds.
These are the materiality and the mentality that do exist in a transitory, impersonal, and interdependent way.
Although Huineng is reprimanding these monks because they're stuck dwelling in forms, it's not to deny that these forms exist.
He's trying to help the monks be liberated from their attachment to sensory objects, including the sensory object of mind.
A hundred and fifty years later, in 880, the nun Miao Shin expounds the Dharma using this koan and awakens 17 monks.
These 17 monks travel to her Zen master's monastery.
They arrive too late, though, to find the mountain, and she was the director of the guest house.
She was there at the guest house when these 17 monks arrived, and they were arguing and debating about this koan.

She overhears this debate, and she says to her attendant, "What a shame that these 17 blind donkeys have worn out so many pairs of straw sandals on their pilgrimage and cannot even dream about the Buddha Dharma."
Her attendant tells the monks what Miao Shin said, and the monks were humbled.
They were sincere in their search for enlightenment, so they bowed respectfully to Miao Shin, and they approached her.
She said, "Please come closer."
But before they could get close enough, she shouted at them, "The wind is not moving, the flag is not moving, the mind is not moving."
And all 17 monks immediately awakened, and they became Miao Shin's disciples.
They returned home without ever even climbing the mountain to see her Zen master.
Now, 150 years later, we have 17 points of view about the flag and the wind, right?
I like this because I'm sure we have all done this ourselves, and we've probably listened to our parents and grandparents and other friends and relatives repeat stories over and over again, right?
Here are these 17 monks picking up this koan, arguing about flag versus wind, and they didn't even directly experience this particular flag or this flapping in that particular wind.
It's not even their own personal experience.
It's a further abstraction of a story.
Ironically, they're arguing about the grand master's teaching without realizing that they too are stuck in dualistic analysis.
This happens when we rely on inverted views, when we forget to investigate our beliefs and uproot our identities.
These monks are fixated on sense objects.

They're fixated on this sense object known as this story of this koan, and what underlies these fixations and points of view, especially if they are chronic and intense, is an attitude, a settled way of thinking or feeling about someone or something that's reflected in our behavior.
These monks are blind to the liberation that's inherent in the present moment.
They're not working with the Buddha mind in each moment of thought.
Both Huineng and Miao Shen are emphasizing direct experience into the nature of mind.
This direct insight is called can show.
Can is seeing, show is nature or essence.
The present moment does not hide the principle, or does not hide Buddha nature.
These 17 monks are not working with Buddha mind in every moment of thought, like I said.
Instead, they're being duped by the proliferations of small minds.
The Buddha calls this habit of mind that leads to conflict, and you could say, well, they're just arguing about a flag and wind, it's no big deal.
But this habit of mind that leads to conflict is called papancha, P-A-N-C-H-A, in Sanskrit.
Thanissaro Bhikkhu, who is a teacher in the Thai forest tradition, says that this word is not so clearly defined in the Buddha's discourses.
However, it's always associated with negative connotations and thoughts about craving, conceit, and views.

Some agreed-upon definitions are conceptual proliferation, flag versus mind, let's argue about it 150 years later; obsessive or repetitive thinking; exaggeration; distortion; and thinking about oneself.
Arguing about whether the flag is moving or the mind is moving might be trivial, like I said.
However, this fundamental proclivity of mind to proliferate when there's a strong sense of self identified with a point of view.
So, We defend our points of view as if our lives depend on them because we wrongly believe that sense objects, and the stories we've created, which of course are also sense objects, are who we are.
This is a fundamental wrong view rooted in ignorance.
As the Heart Sutra says, far beyond all inverted views, one realizes nirvana.
The Pali word for ignorance is vija, V-I-J-J-A.
It means the absence of accurate knowledge.
A vija, the absence of accurate knowledge.
At the heart of ignorance is this conceit of a thinker, a sense of ourselves as a solid, independent, abiding I am, separate.
In one of the Buddha's short sutras, called [unclear: "quickly"], he says the way to establish peace is to put an entire stop to the root of objectification classifications.
I am the thinker, he goes on to say, touched by contact in various ways.
This is how we see the world: we contact the world through the aggregates.
A monk should not keep theorizing about self, with all the proliferations that happen, the sense of contraction of self.
But still, right within, a monk shouldn't seek peace from another.
This is again the Diamond Sutra, Huineng's teaching, unsupported by anything.
For once we're stilled right within, there's nothing embraced, meaning there's no self that we're embracing, no self that we're holding onto and defending.
So how could that be rejected?
How could our points of view be rejected if we really uproot the sense of self?
In this other sutra, called the Honey Ball Sutra, Buddha says that if we're able to not embrace or cling to the sense of self, then this false self won't feel rejected.
And this will end the obsessions of passion, resistance, views, conceit, and ignorance.
The Buddha goes on to say that this is the end of taking up rods and blades, of quarrels and divisive and false speech.
That is where these evil, unskillful things cease without remainder.

For me, Huineng and Myaoshin's teachings are about dissolving the barriers in our own heart minds, dropping fixed views, and investigating whether my perceptions are causing suffering to myself or to others.
Am I experiencing distress or liberation?
If there's an experience of distress, really investigate what's going on here.
Are my perceptions coming from a sense of unity or from division?
Am I blindly believing in something?
Further on in the Honey Ball Sutra, the Buddha talks about the perceptual process and how it can lead to conflict.
This papancha.
Even just from making contact with our eyes with the form, like a flag or a wind, we can start to experience this conflict arising within ourselves.
Here's my rephrasing of the Buddha's analysis with some contemporary references.
When the eye meets a form, eye consciousness arises.
This contact gives rise to neutral, pleasant, or unpleasant feelings.

For some people, if they see an American flag waving in the wind, it evokes feelings of patriotism, feelings of willingness to defend the concept of American values against those who threaten this concept of American values.
Or even back in the day, I'm sure some of you remember when people were burning the flag, and the outrage that caused many people.
All it is is just cloth with these different colors, but it's the symbol of America.
The symbol is being confused with America, in my opinion.
America being a concept as well.
So, when some people see the American flag flapping in the wind, they feel patriotic and loyal to a certain set of American values.

However, other people may see the flag flapping in the wind and have lots of unpleasant feelings associated with the American flag, especially if they are Indigenous people who lived on Turtle Island way before the colonizers and settlers showed up and decimated their people.
So this American flag doesn't evoke the same loyalty.
It can evoke aversion in certain people.
On either side, whether you're pro-American flag or anti-American flag, if you will, what each person feels, they perceive or label in the mind.
And then they think about it.
Forgive me for creating a verb out of papancha, but they papanchais, if you will.

People with similar fixed views and attitudes or identities tend to congregate together, and this amplifies and reifies our leanings, our political leanings, our cultural leanings, our religious leanings.
So this often maybe helps to amplify those views rather than investigate or undermine those views.

It's important, of course, to recognize our differences and appreciate our differences, but I'm wondering how we can do this to bring ourselves closer to understanding each other and cultivating compassion.
How can we drop our fixed views of people who live in red states or who live in blue states?
How can we take the backward step and investigate the one that's perceiving?
Huineng and Miao Shen are pointing to that which animates both the flag and the wind.
That which animates the Republicans, Democrats, independents, anarchists, people who are MAGA, people who are Black Lives Matter.
Whatever flag we happen to be holding, that which animates everybody, everything.
Or, Dogen says, the wisdom that runs through all things.
This has no boundaries, no perspectives, and continues without a trace.
So how can we feel the wind or see the flag [unclear: "on minds"], associative proliferations?
Or how can we drop those associative proliferations?
It's not about ceasing to think.

It's just about not getting caught up in the thinking, not identifying with the thinking. [unclear: "Tapping in the wind, moving"], just be allowed to arise, persist, and perish without clinging or dwelling, without contriving stories that we have to defend.
I'll end with Huineng's awakening verse that earned him the dharma mind seal.
*Bodhi fundamentally has no tree.
The bright mirror also has no stand.
Fundamentally, there is not a single thing.
Where could any dust alight?*
Thank you, everyone.
So, Chris, should I end with the chant before question and response?
Okay.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true America of the Buddha's way.* [unclear: "To be coming"]
